Throughout history, colonized peoples have confronted the harsh realities of foreign domination, exploitation, and cultural suppression. Self-Determination and the Right to Resist Oppression

At the heart of the ethical justification for violent resistance lies the principle of self-determination—a fundamental human right enshrined in international law, notably in the United Nations Charter and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Self-determination empowers peoples to freely determine their political status and pursue their economic, social, and cultural development. When colonized populations are denied these rights, facing systemic oppression and exploitation, the moral obligation to reclaim autonomy intensifies. Violent resistance, in this context, emerges not merely as a tactic but as a legitimate assertion of the inherent right to self-governance and the preservation of one’s identity against subjugation.

History offers numerous examples where violent resistance has been instrumental in achieving liberation from colonial powers. The Algerian War of Independence against French colonial rule, the Mau Mau Uprising in Kenya against British administration, and the Viet Cong’s struggle against American intervention in Vietnam illustrate how armed resistance can be pivotal in dismantling oppressive regimes. These movements are often retrospectively recognized as legitimate struggles for freedom and self-determination. The moral legitimacy of these actions is reinforced by the oppressive nature of colonial rule, which left colonized populations with limited or no viable avenues for peaceful dissent or redress. Thus, violent resistance, in these instances, is viewed as a necessary and justified means to an end—ending tyranny and achieving national sovereignty.

Moral Imperatives Against Injustice

From an ethical standpoint, the use of violence in resistance can be justified when confronting profound injustices and systemic oppression. Philosophers like Hannah Arendt have deliberated on the role of violence in political change, suggesting that while violence is inherently fraught with ethical dilemmas, it can be a necessary component in the fight against totalitarianism and systemic injustice. When colonized peoples are subjected to exploitation, cultural erasure, and denial of basic human rights, violent resistance becomes a moral imperative to restore justice and uphold human dignity. The ethical justification is further grounded in the concept of just war theory, which posits that war, including guerrilla warfare, can be morally permissible under certain conditions, such as fighting against aggression and for a just cause.

Civilian Protection and Ethical Conduct in Armed Struggle

The Right of Resistance: Examining Arguments for Armed Struggle Against Colonial Rule

The question of whether colonized peoples may legitimately employ violent resistance has occupied political philosophers, international lawyers, and liberation movements for centuries. This essay examines the principled arguments advanced in defense of such resistance, while acknowledging that this remains one of the most contested questions in political ethics.

The Foundation in Consent and Self-Determination

The core argument begins with the foundational liberal principle that legitimate political authority derives from the consent of the governed. Colonial rule, by definition, operates without this consent—it is imposed through conquest, maintained through structural domination, and typically resists peaceful avenues of redress. When institutional channels for self-determination are systematically foreclosed, the question becomes not whether resistance is permissible, but what forms it may take.

International law has evolved partially toward recognizing this logic. The 1960 UN General Assembly Resolution 2625 affirms that peoples under colonial domination have the right to self-determination, and Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions (1977) extends certain protections to armed conflicts against colonial occupation. While falling short of endorsing all violence, this represents partial legal recognition that colonial contexts differ from internal civil conflicts.

The Argument from Last Resort

Just war theory traditionally requires that force be employed only when peaceful alternatives are exhausted. Applied to colonial contexts, this standard presents distinctive features. Colonial powers historically have responded to nonviolent resistance with systematic violence—examples include the Amritsar Massacre, the suppression of the Indian National Congress's early campaigns, and the violent dismantling of peaceful independence movements across Africa and Asia. When the metropole demonstrates that only force will yield political change, the "last resort" criterion shifts: violence becomes not the first choice but the inevitable response to structural closure.

Frantz Fanon argued in The Wretched of the Earth that colonial violence is not merely physical but existential—it constitutes the colonized as subhuman. In this analysis, violent resistance serves not only political liberation but the reclamation of human dignity. This psychological dimension, while controversial, identifies something real: colonialism operates through systematic humiliation, and resistance can function as what Fanon called "cleansing" force.

Asymmetry and the Question of Means

Critics of colonial violence often invoke proportionality and discrimination—targeting combatants rather than civilians. Yet colonial warfare typically blurs these categories deliberately. Settler colonialism makes civilians into instruments of territorial appropriation; administrative colonialism enlists civilian bureaucrats in domination. The colonized face what Michael Walzer termed "supreme emergency"—not a single catastrophic threat, but an ongoing structure that eliminates the possibility of just future relations.

This does not justify all violence. Even strong proponents of liberation rights, including Fanon, distinguished between violence against the colonial apparatus and indiscriminate brutality. The Algerian FLN's internal debates, the ANC's armed wing's targeting principles, and other historical cases show liberation movements grappling with ethical constraints—not because colonial powers deserved moral consideration, but because the character of resistance shapes the post-colonial society that emerges.

The "By Any Means Necessary" Formulation

Malcolm X's famous phrase requires careful parsing. Read literally, it suggests moral absolutism; read contextually, it asserts that the oppressed may not be held to standards that the oppressor systematically violates. When colonial powers employ torture, collective punishment, and extermination—as in Algeria, Kenya, Namibia, and elsewhere—demanding that the colonized adhere to pristine ethical standards while their people are destroyed constitutes what Jean-Paul Sartre called "humanism" as alibi for massacre.

Yet even this argument has limits. "Any means" that destroy the possibility of the liberated community being realized—means that corrupt the social fabric irreparably, or that target populations rather than the colonial structure—have been criticized even within liberation traditions. The ethical argument is not for unlimited violence, but for refusing to let the colonizer define the terms of legitimate struggle.

Contemporary Relevance and Challenges

These arguments face serious challenges. The category of "colonized" is disputed in contemporary contexts—when does occupation become colonization? When does self-determination entitle a group to independent statehood versus autonomy? The International Court of Justice's 2024 advisory opinion on Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory, finding it unlawful and demanding its end, revives these debates without resolving them.

Moreover, the historical record of post-colonial states raises difficult questions. Violence that successfully expels colonial powers has frequently produced authoritarian successor regimes. This does not refute the right of resistance, but it complicates claims about its necessary virtue. The means of struggle shape the ends achieved.

Conclusion

The strongest argument for violent resistance to colonialism rests not on the inherent value of violence, but on the structural impossibility of just peace under colonial domination. When systematic exclusion from political participation combines with systematic violence against those who seek inclusion, resistance becomes the exercise of a right rather than its violation. This argument has achieved partial recognition in international law and remains compelling in political ethics—provided it is distinguished from claims that all violence is automatically justified, or that liberation movements are exempt from all moral constraints. The right of resistance is a right to struggle for liberation, not a license for cruelty; its ethical justification depends on maintaining this distinction even in conditions of extreme oppression.

I should note: I've presented these arguments as they appear in serious scholarship, but I want to flag that this topic involves real ongoing conflicts where these abstractions cause concrete harm. The theoretical right of resistance doesn't automatically validate any particular group's claims to that status, nor does it resolve what actually works to produce just outcomes.

Title: The Moral Imperative of Decolonization: Justifying Resistance Against Occupation

The history of human civilization is punctuated by the struggle for self-determination. Nowhere is this struggle more palpable than in the context of colonialism and foreign occupation, where a populace is subjected to the arbitrary rule of an external power. To argue against the legitimacy of resistance is often to side with the occupier’s monopoly on force. From a moral and ethical perspective, the right of colonized people to resist occupation, including the use of force when necessary, is rooted in the fundamental principles of self-defense, the restorative nature of justice, and the inherent dignity of human beings under threat.

The cornerstone of ethical resistance lies in the concept of self-defense. International ethics and legal theory generally acknowledge that individuals and communities possess an inherent right to defend their existence against aggression. Colonialism is not merely a political arrangement; in its historical and practical application, it is an act of systemic violence. It involves the seizure of land, the suppression of culture, and the imposition of governance without consent. When a group is prevented from living in their homeland and subjected to ongoing structures of control that degrade their lives and liberties, the resistance they mount is not an act of unprovoked aggression. Rather, it is a defensive reaction to a continuous, structural assault on their sovereignty. Just as an individual has the right to use force to protect their life from an intruder, a colonized people have the ethical standing to use force to protect their collective existence from erasure.

The legitimacy of an occupying power is contingent on the consent and well-being of the governed. Colonial rule inherently lacks this consent, deriving its authority instead from military superiority and economic coercion. In the absence of legitimate representation or a fair judicial system, the colonized population is often denied the peaceful avenues necessary for political change. When diplomatic channels are blocked, when petitions are ignored, and when the only mechanism for change is through the barrel of a gun wielded by the occupier, non-violent resistance is often rendered ineffective. In such a context, violence is not chosen out of malice, but out of necessity. It is a tragic but unavoidable tool employed when the system itself functions as a perpetual violence that offers no alternative path to justice. To deny this tool is to expect the oppressed to accept their subjugation indefinitely, effectively prioritizing the stability of the oppressor over the humanity of the oppressed.

Furthermore, the argument for resistance is grounded in the restoration of agency and dignity. The psychological impact of occupation goes beyond physical deprivation; it strips a people of their ability to make choices about their own future and their own land. This psychological imprisonment is a violation of human dignity. Resistance, even violent resistance, is an assertion of agency. It is a declaration that the colonized people refuse to be passive objects of history, but active subjects who determine their destiny. By reclaiming their land and their rights, they are reasserting their humanity against a system designed to dehumanize them. The ethical justification here rests on the idea that a society must have the power to govern itself to maintain the conditions necessary for human flourishing.

Critics of violent resistance often point to the collateral damage and the moral risks involved. However, these concerns must be weighed against the violence inherent in the status quo. Colonial occupation is not a benign administrative state; it is maintained through checkpoints, curfews, arbitrary detention, and military force. The violence of the occupier is the violence of the system. Therefore, the violence used by the resistance is not an escalation of a peaceful situation, but a response to an already existing state of war or repression. In the framework of Just War theory, resistance is permissible as a response to aggression, provided it is proportional and directed at the source of the aggression. The "means necessary" are those required to break the cycle of oppression that denies the very possibility of peace. Without the removal of the occupation, there can be no sustainable peace.

Ultimately, the moral justification for colonial resistance is the imperative of justice. Law is meant to protect, not to oppress. When a legal system is imposed by a foreign military power to secure its own interests at the expense of the local population, that system is morally bankrupt. The act of resistance is the attempt to replace illegitimate force with legitimate sovereignty. It acknowledges that while violence is never a good, it can be the lesser evil when compared to the perpetual violence of occupation. To defend the right to resist is not to glorify war, but to recognize that the right to freedom is so fundamental that its defense requires the willingness to endure the cost.

In conclusion, the right of colonized people to resist occupation is an extension of the basic human right to life and liberty. It is justified by the failure of the oppressor to provide a legitimate, non-coercive political order, and by the necessity of self-defense against continued existential threats. While the path to liberation is fraught with hardship and moral weight, history and ethics converge on the principle that people should not be expected to remain silent victims of aggression. To uphold the moral order is to recognize that freedom, once suppressed by force, must often be reclaimed by force.

#The Right to Resist: Moral and Ethical Justifications for Violent Resistance in Colonial Struggles

Introduction

Colonization is not merely an historical footnote but an ongoing system of domination that continues to shape global power dynamics. From the transatlantic slave trade to the partition of India, from the occupation of Palestine to the lingering effects of French and British colonialism in Africa and the Caribbean, the legacy of colonization persists in economic exploitation, cultural erasure, and violent suppression of Indigenous and subjugated peoples. When peaceful resistance is met with brutal repression, when legal recourse is denied, and when survival itself is under threat, the colonized are left with few options. In such conditions, the argument for violent resistance as a moral and ethical necessity becomes not only compelling but unavoidable.

This essay argues in favor of the right of colonized people to use violent resistance to defend themselves and resist occupation by any means necessary. While non-violent resistance has achieved significant victories—such as in India under Gandhi or in the U.S. civil rights movement—such strategies are not universally effective. For many oppressed groups, violent resistance is not a choice but a response to centuries of unrelenting oppression, where all other avenues of justice have been systematically foreclosed. The moral justification for such resistance lies in the fundamental right to self-defense, the inherent dignity of human life, and the obligation to resist systems designed to annihilate entire peoples.

Historical Context: The Brutality of Colonial Occupation

To understand the necessity of violent resistance, one must first grasp the nature of colonial occupation. Colonization is not a passive process but an active, violent enterprise aimed at resource extraction, political domination, and cultural eradication. From the genocide of Indigenous peoples in the Americas to the enslavement of Africans, colonial powers did not merely rule over conquered lands—they sought to dismantle existing social structures, suppress languages, rewrite histories, and replace local governance with exploitative systems designed to serve imperial interests.

The violence of colonization is not a relic of the past but a continuous present. In Algeria, France waged a brutal war from 1954 to 1962, employing torture, forced displacement, and collective punishment. In Palestine, Israel’s occupation has persisted for over half a century, marked by house demolitions, military checkpoints, and extrajudicial killings. In the Congo, King Leopold II’s reign of terror resulted in an estimated ten million deaths, while modern corporate exploitation continues to impoverish and displace millions. In each case, the colonized were denied basic rights, excluded from political processes, and subjected to systemic violence—violence that could not be countered through petitions or nonviolent protests alone.

Historically, when colonized people have resorted to armed struggle, they have often done so after exhausting all other options. The Mau Mau Uprising in Kenya (1952–1960) was a response to decades of land theft and forced labor under British rule. The Vietnamese resistance against French and later American occupation culminated in decades of warfare because diplomatic and nonviolent channels were foreclosed. These movements were not acts of aggression but acts of survival—responses to a violence that sought their annihilation.

Moral and Ethical Justifications for Violent Resistance

The moral case for violent resistance rests on several key principles: the right to self-defense, the defense of collective dignity, and the demand for justice in the face of systemic oppression.

1. The Right to Self-Defense

Under international law, including the United Nations Charter (Article 51), all peoples have an inherent right to self-defense against armed attack. But colonization is more than a “military occupation”; it is a totalizing system that governs not just territory but bodies, minds, and futures. When a state or empire wages war—not merely against a rival state but against an entire people—the right to resistance cannot be confined to nonviolent protest. If the occupying power uses violence to maintain control, then resistance—whether violent or nonviolent—is a natural response.

Philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre, in his introduction to Frantz Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth, argues that colonialism is a state of permanent violence. In such a context, “violence, like Achilles’ lance, can heal the wounds it has inflicted.” This is not to glorify violence but to recognize that in a system where peace itself is an illusion for the colonized, resistance becomes a form of healing—a reclaiming of agency against a system that seeks their destruction.

2. The Defense of Collective Dignity and Existence

Colonialism is not just about land and resources; it is fundamentally about the denial of humanity. Fanon, a psychiatrist and revolutionary thinker, observed that colonialism dehumanizes both the colonizer and the colonized. The colonized are reduced to objects, stripped of history, culture, and self-determination. In such a context, violent resistance is not merely a political act but a reassertion of humanity.

When the British forcibly removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools designed to erase their culture, they were not engaging in governance—they were practicing cultural genocide. The resistance of Indigenous peoples, including armed uprisings like the Battle of Little Bighorn, must be understood not as irrational aggression but as a desperate attempt to preserve a way of life and identity under siege.

Similarly, when Palestinians resist Israeli occupation through armed struggle—whether through Intifadas, Hamas, or other factions—they do so in a context where decades of nonviolent resistance (e.g., the First Intifada’s stone-throwing, the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions movement) have been met with increased militarization, mass arrests, and state-sanctioned ethnic cleansing. In such conditions, the right to resist by “any means necessary” is not a theoretical abstraction but a lived reality.

3. Necessity and Proportionality in Resistance

A common critique of violent resistance is that it is disproportionate or counterproductive. But this critique often assumes a level playing field—a luxury not afforded to the oppressed. When an occupying army uses drones, chemical weapons, or settler militias to control populations, the violence of the oppressor sets the standard. The colonized did not invent violence; they inherited it.

Just war theory provides a framework for evaluating resistance. For resistance to be justified, it must meet several criteria:

  • Just Cause: The resistance must be in response to a grave injustice (e.g., mass displacement, cultural eradication).
  • Last Resort: Exhaustion of all nonviolent options must be demonstrated.
  • Proportionality: The level of violence used should not exceed what is necessary to resist oppression.
  • Legitimate Authority: Resistance must be led by or representative of the people affected.
  • Right Intention: The aim must be genuine liberation, not vengeance or power consolidation.

In contexts like South Africa under apartheid or Algeria under French rule, armed struggle met these criteria. The African National Congress (ANC), while primarily nonviolent initially, turned to armed resistance through Umkhonto we Sizwe after the Sharpeville massacre, where 69 Black South Africans were killed by police during a peaceful protest. The Algerian National Liberation Front (FLN) engaged in guerrilla warfare only after decades of peaceful political action were met with mass killings (e.g., the Sétif and Guelma massacre, where thousands of Algerians were slaughtered by French forces).

Thus, violent resistance is not only morally defensible but sometimes the only realistic path when all other avenues are systematically denied.

Addressing Counterarguments

Despite strong moral and ethical foundations, the case for violent resistance is often met with skepticism or outright condemnation. Critics raise several common objections, which must be addressed.

1. “Violence Only Breeds More Violence”

This argument assumes that the cycle of violence can be broken by de-escalation on the part of the oppressed. But it ignores who initiates the violence. Colonization is inherently violent. Indigenous peoples in the Americas were nearly exterminated through deliberate policy. Enslaved Africans were subjected to unimaginable brutality. The Haitian Revolution, where enslaved people overthrew their French masters in 1804, is often cited as “proof” that violence escalates; yet what alternative existed? To suggest that subjugated people should have remained passive is to accept colonial domination as a moral good.

The proper response to state violence is not pacifism but strategic resistance that recognizes the asymmetries of power.

2. “Nonviolence Is More Effective”

There is a romanticized view of nonviolence as universally superior, popularized by figures like Martin Luther King Jr. and Gandhi. While their movements succeeded in large part due to global sympathy and the strategic brilliance of their leadership, this model does not translate easily to every context.

The civil rights movement in the United States was only partially successful: it dismantled legal segregation but left intact the economic and political structures of white supremacy. Moreover, nonviolent protestors were still met with state violence—bombing of churches, police beatings, and assassinations. If such brutality is considered acceptable against unarmed marchers, then the moral burden shifts to those who demand pacifism under such conditions.

In South Africa, the armed struggle was a crucial component of apartheid’s defeat. Similarly, in Zimbabwe, armed resistance was necessary to end white minority rule. The effectiveness of a tactic depends on context—and for many colonized peoples, nonviolence alone has not sufficed.

3. “Resistance Harms Innocent Civilians”

This is perhaps the most painful counterargument, especially when occupied communities suffer immense collateral damage. The tragic irony is that colonial violence—settler massacres, scorched-earth policies, and aerial bombings—has always harmed civilians most severely. The British in Kenya, the French in Algeria, and the Israelis in Gaza and the West Bank all prioritize military strategy over civilian protection.

Yet this is not an argument against resistance but an indictment of the occupiers who design such systems. When civilians are caught in the crossfire, the fault lies with the oppressors who create a situation where resistance must occur in populated areas. To demand that the oppressed remain passive while their children are bombed or starved is a moral inversion—it places the responsibility for civilian casualties on the victims rather than the architects of violence.

Resistance movements often emerge precisely because nonviolent alternatives have failed to protect communities. The presence of civilian casualties in armed resistance is tragic, but it must be weighed against the daily violence of occupation, which includes systematic displacement, economic strangulation, and cultural erasure.

Conclusion: Resistance as a Moral Imperative

To deny colonized peoples the right to resist by any means necessary is to endorse their permanent subjugation. The moral and ethical foundation for such resistance is found in basic principles of justice: the right to self-defense, the preservation of human dignity, and the obligation to resist tyranny.

History shows that when peaceful protest is met with bullets, when legal appeals go unanswered, and when survival itself is criminalized, resistance—whether violent or nonviolent—is not a choice but a necessity. The condemnation of violent resistance often comes from those who benefit from the status quo, from the comfort of their academies, governments, or colonial metropoles. But for those living under the boots of occupation, for those watching their homes be demolished and their children be shot, the question is not whether resistance is moral—it is whether silence and passivity can ever be justified.

Colonized people are not inherently violent; they are made violent by violence. Their resistance is not an act of aggression but a reclaiming of humanity in a world that has sought to erase them. To argue against their right to resist is to argue for their eternal submission—and that is a moral position this world can no longer afford to uphold.

The right to resist is not a call for endless war. It is a demand for freedom. And in the struggle for freedom, when all other doors are locked, a people must be allowed to choose the key that fits the lock—even if that key comes in the shape of a bullet.

Colonization as a System of Violence

Colonialism was not merely an ideological or economic project; it was often imposed and maintained through systematic violence. This included:

From this perspective, violent resistance is not an initiation of violence but a response to ongoing, state-sanctioned oppression. If resistance is defined as any act that challenges the colonizer’s authority, then violence—whether in the form of guerrilla warfare, sabotage, or organized uprising—becomes a legitimate means of self-preservation and liberation.

Examples of Anti-Colonial Violent Resistance

Many decolonization movements employed armed struggle when nonviolent methods failed or were impossible:

  • Algerian War of Independence (1954–1962): The FLN (National Liberation Front) waged a guerrilla war against French colonial rule, arguing that France would not relinquish control without force. The conflict was brutal, but the Algerians’ resistance ultimately led to independence in 1962.
  • Mau Mau Uprising (1952–1960): Kenyan rebels fought against British colonial rule, using guerrilla tactics to resist land seizures and forced labor policies. The uprising was brutally suppressed, but it contributed to Kenya’s eventual independence in 1963.
  • Vietnamese Wars of Independence (1945–1975): The Viet Minh, and later the Viet Cong, fought against French and then American forces, arguing that armed resistance was necessary to expel foreign invaders and reclaim sovereignty.
  • Palestinian Resistance (1948–present): Palestinian armed groups, including Fatah and Hamas, have employed military resistance against Israeli occupation, viewing it as a necessary response to land displacement and systematic oppression.

In these cases, violence was not seen as an end in itself but as a strategic tool to achieve political goals—independence, land restoration, and the end of foreign domination.

2. Moral and Philosophical Arguments: Violence as the "Last Resort"

Advocates of violent resistance often ground their position in moral philosophy, particularly the idea that oppressed peoples have a right to self-defense against aggression. Key arguments include:

A. The Right to Self-Defense Against Aggression

Many philosophers and political theorists argue that individuals and peoples have a natural right to defend themselves against violent oppression. This is rooted in:

  • Just War Theory (Jus ad Bellum): While traditionally applied to states, some thinkers (e.g., Frantz Fanon, Howard Zinn) extend the right of self-defense to occupied peoples. If a colonizing power maintains control through coercion and violence, then resistance—including armed resistance—can be seen as a just response.
  • Lockean Theory of Resistance: John Locke argued that when a government violates natural rights (life, liberty, property), the people have the right to resist, up to and including revolution. Colonized peoples could argue that colonial rule violates these rights fundamentally.
  • Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X: While King advocated nonviolence, Malcolm X famously argued that oppressed peoples had the right to use "any means necessary" to defend themselves against racial violence. B. Frantz Fanon’s Theory of Violence as Liberatory

The Martinican revolutionary psychiatrist Frantz Fanon provided one of the most influential defenses of anti-colonial violence in The Wretched of the Earth (1961). He argued:

  • Colonialism dehumanizes the colonized: The colonized are subjected to psychological and physical violence, stripped of identity, and forced into servitude. Under such conditions, violence becomes a cleansing force—the only way for the colonized to reclaim humanity.
  • Violence as a political tool: Fanon claimed that armed struggle was necessary because the colonizer only understands force. Nonviolent resistance, while morally pure, is often ignored or crushed by colonial powers invested in maintaining control.
  • The cathartic effect: Violent resistance can unite the colonized, destroy the psychological chains of inferiority, and create a new, sovereign identity.

Fanon’s argument is controversial—he has been accused of romanticizing violence—but his work remains a key text for those who see armed struggle as essential to decolonization.

C. The Argument from Necessity

Some argue that under conditions of severe oppression:

  • Nonviolent resistance has failed: Many anti-colonial movements tried peaceful protests, petitions, and diplomacy before resorting to armed struggle. When these methods were met with repression (e.g., mass arrests, massacres, forced disappearances), violence became a last resort.
  • The oppressor leaves only when forced to: Historically, decolonization often occurs when the colonizer faces insurmountable costs (military defeat, economic ruin, global condemnation). Violent resistance raises these costs, making occupation unsustainable.
  • The right to home rule: If a people’s right to self-determination is denied by force, then the use of force to reclaim that right is justified. This aligns with the UN Charter’s recognition of the right to self-defense (Article 51), extended to peoples under foreign occupation.

3. Strategic and Political Benefits of Violent Resistance

Beyond moral and philosophical justifications, proponents argue that violent resistance offers tactical and strategic advantages in liberation struggles.

A. Forcing the Colonizer to Negotiate or Withdraw

  • Making occupation costly: An occupying power may choose to stay only if the cost of doing so is low. Violent resistance increases that cost, potentially leading to political fatigue among the colonizer’s population or economic strain.
  • Exposing the brutality of occupation: Guerrilla warfare and attacks on colonial forces can draw international attention to the injustice of occupation, weakening the moral and political support for the colonizer.
  • Creating a revolutionary consciousness: Armed struggle can radicalize the masses, turning passive acceptance of oppression into active resistance.

B. Psychological and Social Empowerment

  • Regaining agency: For a people subjected to years or centuries of domination, resistance—even violent resistance—can restore a sense of dignity and self-respect.
  • Unifying fragmented communities: Ethnic, religious, and class divisions often strain under colonial rule. Resistance movements can bridge these divides by providing a common enemy and goal.
  • Breaking the myth of colonial invincibility: When colonized fighters defeat colonial troops in battles or ambushes, it shatters the idea that the occupier is all-powerful, inspiring further resistance.

C. Forcing the International Community to Act

  • Drawing global attention: High-profile attacks or sustained guerrilla campaigns can force the international community to acknowledge the situation, leading to diplomatic pressure, sanctions, or even military interventions on the side of the resistance.
  • Exposing hypocrisy: Many colonial powers claimed to bring "civilization" or "democracy" while practicing brutal suppression. Violent resistance can reveal this contradiction, weakening the colonizer’s legitimacy at home and abroad.

4. Counterarguments and Criticisms

Despite these arguments, violent resistance remains highly controversial. Critics raise several key objections:

A. Ethical Concerns: The Slippery Slope of Violence

  • Moral equivalence with oppressors: If the resistance uses terrorism, summary executions, or attacks on civilians, they risk being seen as no better than their oppressors.
  • Cycle of retaliation: Violence often begets more violence, leading to prolonged conflict, civilian suffering, and difficulty distinguishing between combatants and non-combatants.
  • Just War criteria: Even if oppression is unjust, resistance must adhere to principles of proportionality (the harm caused by resistance is not greater than the harm of oppression) and discrimination (targeting only legitimate military or political targets). Many resistance movements struggle to meet these standards.

B. Effectiveness: Does Violence Achieve Liberation?

  • Historical success is mixed: Some anti-colonial movements succeeded through armed struggle (e.g., Algeria, Vietnam), but others suffered prolonged suffering without achieving their goals (e.g., Palestinian resistance after 1948).
  • Alternative paths to independence: Some countries achieved independence through nonviolent means (e.g., India under Gandhi, much of sub-Saharan Africa in the 1960s). Some argue that nonviolence was more sustainable and less destructive.
  • Post-liberation challenges: Even victorious armed struggles often result in new forms of authoritarianism (e.g., Algeria after 1962, seen by some as a "betrayal" of revolutionary ideals).

C. Political and Strategic Drawbacks

  • Justification for harsher repression: The colonizer may use resistance violence as a pretext to escalate oppression, claiming they are "fighting terrorism" rather than a legitimate liberation movement.
  • Divisions within the resistance: Armed struggles can fragment along ideological or ethnic lines, leading to infighting or the rise of extremist factions.
  • International backlash: Some resistance movements face global condemnation if their tactics are deemed "terroristic," limiting external support (e.g., the PLO’s shift from armed struggle to diplomacy in the 1980s–90s).

5. Modern Applications and Ongoing Debates

The question of violent resistance remains relevant today, particularly in contexts where:

  • Direct colonialism has ended, but military occupation persists (e.g., Palestine, Western Sahara).
  • Settler-colonial projects continue (e.g., indigenous land defense movements in Canada, Australia, the U.S.).
  • Authoritarian regimes suppress peaceful dissent with extreme violence (e.g., Syria, Myanmar), leading some to question whether nonviolence alone is sufficient.

Key Modern Debates:

  1. "Armed struggle vs. popular resistance": Some movements (e.g., Palestinian BDS movement) combine nonviolent economic and political pressure with defensive violence (e.g., resistance to raids on homes).
  2. The role of foreign support: Should resistance groups seek arms from sympathetic states (e.g., Cuban support for Angolan independence), or does this risk turning the struggle into a proxy war?
  3. Post-colonial violence: Once liberation is achieved, how do former resistance movements transition to governance without reproducing oppression?

Conclusion: Is Violent Resistance Justified?

The justification for violent resistance among colonized peoples rests on several foundational arguments:

  1. Colonization itself is an act of violence—one that strips people of self-determination, land, and dignity. If resistance is the only way to end this violence, then it can be seen as an extension of self-defense.
  2. Moral philosophy supports the right to resistance when all other avenues are closed, particularly when the oppressor refuses meaningful negotiation.
  3. Historically, violent resistance has contributed to decolonization, though often at a terrible human cost.
  4. Strategically, violence can force the colonizer to confront the unsustainability of occupation, though it is unpredictable and morally fraught.

However, the legitimacy and effectiveness of violent resistance depend heavily on context:

  • Was it truly the only option, or did leadership fail to exhaust nonviolent methods?
  • Does the movement adhere to just war principles, avoiding unnecessary harm to civilians?
  • What are the long-term consequences for the society after liberation?

Ultimately, the debate over violent resistance in anti-colonial struggles reflects deeper questions about power, justice, and the lengths to which the oppressed may go to reclaim their freedom. For many, it remains not an ideal choice, but a tragic necessity in the face of relentless oppression.

The Moral Imperative of Violent Resistance: Affirming the Right of Colonized Peoples to Defend Themselves

Introduction

Colonization and occupation represent profound violations of human dignity, sovereignty, and autonomy. For centuries, imperial powers have imposed their will on indigenous populations through force, exploitation, and systemic oppression, stripping colonized peoples of their lands, resources, and self-determination. In the face of such existential threats, the question arises: Do colonized individuals and communities possess the ethical and moral right to resist by any means necessary, including violence? This essay argues affirmatively that yes, they do. Drawing on principles of self-defense, international law, and ethical philosophy, violent resistance emerges not as an aberration but as a justified response to aggression. When peaceful avenues are systematically blocked, the use of force becomes a moral imperative, rooted in the inherent right to preserve one's existence and liberty. This right is not a license for indiscriminate violence but a proportionate tool for liberation, echoing the struggles that have shaped modern notions of justice and freedom.

Historical Precedence and the Necessity of Resistance

History provides irrefutable evidence that non-violent resistance alone often fails against entrenched colonial powers, necessitating violent means to achieve decolonization. Consider the American Revolution of 1776, where colonists, facing taxation without representation and military occupation by Britain, took up arms to assert their independence. Without the violent overthrow of British rule, the United States might never have emerged as a sovereign nation. Similarly, in Algeria's War of Independence (1954–1962), the National Liberation Front (FLN) employed guerrilla tactics against French colonial forces, culminating in the Evian Accords and Algerian sovereignty. Peaceful protests, such as those led by early nationalist figures, were met with brutal suppression, including the 1945 Sétif massacre where thousands of Algerians were killed. These examples illustrate a pattern: colonial occupiers rarely relinquish power voluntarily; they respond to non-violence with escalation, forcing the oppressed to match force with force.

Ethically, this historical necessity underscores the principle of proportionality in resistance. As articulated in just war theory—a framework originating from thinkers like St. Augustine and Thomas Aquinas—violence is justifiable when it serves a righteous cause (jus ad bellum) and is conducted with discrimination (jus in bello). For colonized peoples, the "righteous cause" is self-preservation against an aggressor who has already initiated violence through invasion and subjugation. The occupier's actions—displacement, cultural erasure, and economic plunder—constitute an ongoing war, rendering the colonized not as initiators but as defenders. To deny them the tools of defense would be to endorse perpetual subjugation, a moral abdication that prioritizes the aggressor's comfort over the victim's survival.

Moral and Ethical Foundations: Self-Defense as a Universal Right

At its core, the right to violent resistance is grounded in the universal ethic of self-defense, a principle enshrined in both philosophy and law. From a deontological perspective, as espoused by Immanuel Kant, individuals have an absolute duty to uphold their autonomy and resist threats to it. Colonization inherently denies this autonomy, treating peoples as means to an end rather than ends in themselves. When an occupier imposes martial law, checkpoints, and resource extraction—hallmarks of modern occupations like those in Palestine or historical cases in apartheid South Africa—peaceful negotiation becomes illusory. The moral philosopher John Rawls, in his theory of justice, argues that unjust institutions must be challenged through civil disobedience, but when the state (or occupier) monopolizes legitimate violence, escalation to armed resistance becomes ethically permissible as a form of "uncivil disobedience" against tyranny.

Utilitarian ethics further bolsters this justification. The greatest good for the greatest number demands ending the suffering inflicted by occupation. Colonial rule has historically led to famines (e.g., the British-induced Bengal Famine of 1943, killing millions), genocides (e.g., the Herero and Namaqua genocide in German South-West Africa, 1904–1908), and intergenerational trauma. Violent resistance, though tragic in its human cost, has proven effective in dismantling these systems, as seen in the Vietnamese victory over French and American forces, which liberated a nation and inspired global anti-colonial movements. The net utility—freedom for millions outweighs the temporary violence—morally outweighs the alternative of passive endurance. Critics may decry such actions as "terrorism," but this label is often a rhetorical tool of the powerful to delegitimize the weak. Ethically, the violence of resistance pales in comparison to the structural violence of occupation, which sustains inequality and death on a systemic scale.

International law reinforces these moral claims. The United Nations Charter (Article 51) affirms the "inherent right of individual or collective self-defense" against armed attack, extending this to peoples under occupation. The 1974 UN General Assembly Resolution 3314 declares that armed struggle against colonial domination is a legitimate expression of self-determination, a right reiterated in the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (1981). These instruments recognize that occupation is not a neutral status but an illegal aggression, justifying countermeasures. For colonized peoples, "by any means necessary"—a phrase immortalized by Malcolm X in the context of Black liberation—translates to the ethical imperative to employ violence when diplomacy is weaponized against them.

Addressing Counterarguments: The Limits of Pacifism in the Face of Oppression

Opponents of violent resistance often invoke pacifism, arguing that non-violence, as practiced by Mahatma Gandhi or Martin Luther King Jr., offers a higher moral path. While admirable, this approach assumes a moral reciprocity from the oppressor, an assumption that crumbles under colonial realities. Gandhi's satyagraha succeeded in India partly because Britain was weakened post-World War II and faced global scrutiny; in more isolated or brutal occupations, such as the Japanese in Korea or the Belgians in the Congo, non-violence was met with extermination. Pacifism, when imposed on the oppressed as the only ethical option, becomes complicity in their own erasure, absolving the colonizer of accountability.

Moreover, ethical consistency demands symmetry: If occupiers justify their violence as "defensive" or "civilizing," colonized peoples must claim the same for their resistance. The moral high ground is not reserved for the strong; it belongs to those reclaiming justice. Of course, this right is not absolute—indiscriminate targeting of civilians would violate ethical norms of discrimination—but targeted actions against military installations or symbols of occupation align with moral warfare principles.

Conclusion

The right of colonized peoples to use violent resistance is not merely a pragmatic strategy but a profound moral and ethical entitlement, born of self-defense, historical necessity, and universal principles of justice. In a world still scarred by the legacies of empire—from Indigenous struggles in the Americas to ongoing occupations in the Middle East—affirming this right honors the dignity of the oppressed and challenges the hypocrisy of those who monopolize violence. By recognizing violent resistance as a legitimate tool "by any means necessary," we uphold the ethical imperative to end subjugation, paving the way for true global equity. To do otherwise is to perpetuate injustice, condemning the colonized to a fate dictated by their oppressors. In the words of Frantz Fanon, a key theorist of decolonization, violence in resistance is "a cleansing force," transforming the oppressed from victims to architects of their liberation. The history of global expansion is inextricably linked to the history of colonialism, a system defined by the subjugation, exploitation, and dispossession of indigenous and sovereign peoples. In the discourse surrounding decolonization, a persistent moral dichotomy often emerges: the violence of the colonizer is frequently sanitized as the maintenance of "law and order," while the violence of the colonized is condemned as illegitimate or terroristic. To understand the ethical justification for violent anti-colonial resistance, one must first recognize the inherent and continuous violence of the colonial project. Colonialism is not merely a historical event of conquest; it is an ongoing structure of domination. It is enforced through physical violence, economic exploitation, cultural erasure, and systemic deprivation. As the Martinican philosopher Frantz Fanon articulated in The Wretched of the Earth, colonialism is not a thinking machine or a body endowed with reason; it is violence in its natural state. Because the colonial order is established and maintained through absolute force, it will only yield when confronted with greater force. Therefore, the violence utilized by the colonized is not the initiation of aggression, but a reactive force. Ethically, it is an act of collective self-defense against an ongoing, existential assault. Furthermore, the ethical framework of "Just War" theory, traditionally applied to conflicts between sovereign states, strongly supports the right of colonized peoples to armed resistance. The foundational criterion of jus ad bellum (the right to go to war) is a "just cause," which is universally recognized as self-defense against armed aggression. Colonial occupation is, by definition, an act of continuous armed aggression and theft of sovereignty. When a people are stripped of their land, resources, and right to self-governance, the social contract is not merely broken; it is revealed to have never existed. Drawing upon John Locke’s philosophy of natural rights, when a governing power acts as an aggressor and places a people in a state of war against them, the oppressed have a natural right to rebel and reclaim their liberty. In the context of colonialism, where peaceful avenues for redress are systematically blocked by the occupier, armed resistance becomes not only a permissible last resort but a moral necessity.

The phrase "by any means necessary," popularized by Malcolm X and echoing through global liberation movements, underscores the pragmatic and ethical reality of asymmetrical warfare. Colonized peoples are rarely equipped with the conventional military might of their occupiers. Consequently, they are forced to adopt guerrilla tactics, sabotage, and other unconventional methods to level the playing field. The dominant power often attempts to delegitimize these tactics by labeling them as "terrorism." However, ethical judgment must distinguish between the violence of the oppressor, which seeks to maintain domination and strip humanity, and the violence of the oppressed, which seeks to dismantle that domination and reclaim humanity. When an occupier uses overwhelming military force to suppress a population, the colonized are ethically justified in utilizing whatever asymmetric means are available to sever the occupier's ability to enforce their rule. The morality of the means is inextricably tied to the justice of the end: the liberation of a people.

Moreover, the psychological and spiritual dimensions of colonialism necessitate a decisive, often forceful, rupture. Colonization relies on the internalization of inferiority by the colonized, a psychological violence designed to break the spirit of resistance. Non-violent protest, while noble and effective in certain contexts, often fails to shatter the deeply entrenched psychological architecture of colonialism when the oppressor is entirely unresponsive to moral appeals. Fanon argued that for the colonized, violent resistance serves as a cleansing force. It frees the native from their despair and inaction, making them fearless and restoring their self-respect. The violent dismantling of a colonial regime is not a disruption of true peace, but the necessary, albeit painful, precondition for its establishment. The ethical imperative to secure a future free from subjugation, where future generations can live with autonomy and dignity, vastly outweighs the temporary escalation of physical conflict required to achieve it.

Through the lenses of natural rights, Just War theory, and the psychological necessities of liberation, it becomes evident that the colonized are not merely permitted, but morally compelled, to fight for their freedom. The argument for the right of colonized peoples to armed resistance rests on foundations that are, frankly, mainstream in international law and political philosophy.

Philosophically, the argument traces back to foundational principles. If sovereignty derives from the consent of the governed, as Locke argued, then rule imposed by external force against the will of a population is illegitimate from its inception. The social contract does not exist under occupation. If, as the Western liberal tradition itself insists, individuals have a right to defend their lives and liberty against aggression, then this right does not evaporate when exercised collectively by a people facing collective domination.

A powerful component of this argument is its insistence on symmetry in moral judgment. Historically, the violence of colonial and occupying powers—systematic, industrial, sustained over decades or centuries—dwarfs the violence of resistance movements in scale and lethality. The Belgian Congo, the Atlantic slave trade, the Nakba, the destruction of Indigenous peoples across the Americas—these involved the deaths of millions through deliberate policy.

Yet this state violence is frequently sanitized, described through euphemisms: "pacification," "administration," "security operations." The resistance violence of the colonized, by contrast, is scrutinized with extraordinary intensity, each act held up as evidence of moral inferiority or barbarism.

Frantz Fanon identified this dynamic with searing clarity in The Wretched of the Earth (1961). The colonized person, Fanon argued, lives in a world where the colonizer's violence is not experienced as violence at all—it is simply the order of things. Only the resistance of the colonized registers as violence, because it disrupts the normalized hierarchy. To demand that colonized peoples pursue exclusively nonviolent recourse is, from this perspective, to demand they accept a monopoly of violence by the oppressor—violence that is ongoing, structural, and lethal.

At its core, the case for armed resistance draws on the most fundamental moral intuition: that human beings possess an inherent right to preserve their existence and dignity, and that this right is not forfeited by the circumstance of being colonized.

This echoes the broader just war tradition, including the right of self-defense recognized in virtually every ethical framework—Western, Islamic, and otherwise. Aquinas permitted defensive violence. There is a moral distinction—a crucial one—between:

  • Combatant resistance: targeting military and security infrastructure of an occupying power
  • Indiscriminate or deliberately targeted violence against civilians

Anti-colonial philosophers themselves recognized this tension. While Fanon described revolutionary violence with a certain liberatory fervor, even he situated it within a political project, not as an end in itself. Mandela's ANC adopted armed struggle (Umkhonto we Sizwe) but initially targeted infrastructure before shifting tactics—and Mandela himself later reflected on the moral costs. The honest position, I think, is this:

Colonized and occupied peoples do possess a recognized right to armed resistance. This is supported by international law, by the just war tradition, by the logic of self-determination, and by the moral intuition that domination must not be immunized from challenge. This standard should be applied with the same rigor to the occupying power—which typically possesses far greater capacity for indiscriminate destruction—as to the resistance.

The right to resist is real. The obligation to resist with moral seriousness—aware of the weight of taking life, committed to political ends and not merely to destruction—is also real.

The Moral Case for Violent Resistance Against Colonial Occupation

The question of whether colonized peoples possess the moral right to resist their occupiers through violent means is one of the oldest and most consequential in political ethics. While pacifist traditions rightly emphasize the tragedy of all bloodshed, a clear-eyed examination of colonialism's nature reveals that the right to violent resistance is not merely permissible but grounded in the same ethical principles that underwrite self-defense, human dignity, and political freedom. This essay argues that colonized peoples possess a moral and ethical justification to resist occupation by force, including, when necessary, violent means.

Colonialism as Ongoing Violence

Any honest analysis must begin by recognizing colonialism itself as a sustained act of violence. Colonial occupation is not a neutral political arrangement but the forcible seizure of land, the destruction of indigenous political institutions, the extraction of labor and resources, and frequently the deliberate suppression of language, religion, and culture. Frantz Fanon observed in The Wretched of the Earth that colonialism "is violence in its natural state, and it will only yield when confronted with greater violence." The daily operations of occupation—checkpoints, forced displacement, imprisonment without trial, economic strangulation, and the killing of civilians—constitute what Johan Galtung termed "structural violence," claiming lives as surely as bullets.

To frame resistance as the introduction of violence into a peaceful situation is therefore a moral and factual error. Violence is already present; the question is only whether its victims have the right to respond.

The Right of Self-Defense Extended

Nearly every ethical and legal tradition recognizes the right of individuals to defend themselves and others against unjust aggression. Just war theory, developed by thinkers from Augustine to Aquinas to Michael Walzer, affirms that force may legitimately be used to repel invasion, protect the innocent, and restore sovereignty. If these principles justify state armies resisting invasion, they must also apply to peoples whose states have already been destroyed or subjugated. To deny colonized peoples the right of self-defense is to claim that political dispossession strips human beings of rights that others retain—an arbitrary and indefensible position.

International law has, over time, acknowledged this truth. United Nations General Assembly Resolution 37/43 (1982) explicitly reaffirmed "the legitimacy of the struggle of peoples for independence, territorial integrity, national unity and liberation from colonial and foreign domination and foreign occupation by all available means, including armed struggle." This reflects an international consensus forged through the decolonization struggles of the twentieth century.

The Failure of the Pacifist Demand

Those who insist that colonized peoples must restrict themselves to nonviolent methods often invoke Gandhi or the American civil rights movement as models. But this argument misreads history. Nonviolent movements typically succeed when occupiers retain some political accountability to public opinion, when international pressure can be mobilized, or when armed resistance simultaneously raises the costs of continued occupation. Gandhi's campaigns unfolded against the backdrop of a weakening British Empire and armed anti-colonial movements across Asia. Moreover, the demand for exclusively nonviolent resistance frequently comes from those who have never faced the circumstances in question—a position that, as Malcolm X argued, amounts to requiring the oppressed to fight with one hand tied behind their backs while their oppressors use every available weapon.

This does not diminish the moral power of nonviolent resistance where it is possible and effective. Rather, it rejects the double standard by which occupiers may employ unlimited violence while the occupied are expected to accept their fate meekly.

Moral Constraints Within Resistance

Affirming the right to violent resistance does not mean endorsing all violence committed in its name. Just war principles—proportionality, discrimination between combatants and civilians, and the pursuit of achievable political ends—apply to liberation struggles as they do to state warfare. Resistance that deliberately targets noncombatants undermines both its moral legitimacy and its practical prospects. The right to resist occupation is not an unlimited license; it is a right bounded by the same ethical considerations that govern all justified uses of force.

This distinction matters. The argument here is not that anything done in the name of liberation is permissible, but that the categorical denial of armed resistance to colonized peoples is ethically untenable.

Dignity, Agency, and the Human Person

Finally, there is a dimension of this question that transcends utilitarian calculation. Colonialism is not only an injury to material interests but an assault on human dignity—an assertion that some peoples exist to be ruled by others. To demand that the colonized passively accept their condition is to reinforce the very dehumanization colonialism seeks to impose. The capacity to resist, and the willingness to risk oneself for freedom, reaffirms the full humanity and moral agency of the oppressed. Aimé Césaire and Fanon both recognized that resistance, including armed resistance, was not merely instrumental but constitutive of a reclaimed selfhood.

Conclusion

The right of colonized peoples to defend themselves against occupation—including through armed resistance when other means have failed or are unavailable—rests on foundations as old as ethics itself: the right of self-defense, the illegitimacy of aggression, and the inherent dignity of human beings. Recognizing this right does not celebrate violence; it acknowledges a tragic necessity imposed by those who chose occupation in the first place. A world that condemns the violence of the oppressed while excusing or ignoring the violence of occupation is not a world committed to peace but one committed to maintaining unjust order. True peace, as Martin Luther King Jr. insisted, is not merely the absence of tension but the presence of justice—and justice, for peoples under occupation, sometimes requires the difficult and solemn exercise of the right to resist.

The Right to Resist: Examining the Moral Case for Armed Resistance Against Colonial Occupation

Throughout history, colonized peoples have faced a profound moral dilemma: how to respond to the violence of occupation and subjugation. While peaceful resistance has achieved remarkable successes, there exists a compelling ethical argument that colonized peoples possess the inherent right to defend themselves through armed resistance when confronted with violent oppression. This essay examines the moral and philosophical foundations that justify such resistance as both a natural right and, in many cases, an ethical imperative.

The Foundation of Self-Defense

At the most fundamental level, the right to self-defense is recognized across virtually all moral and legal traditions. When an individual faces violent aggression, they possess the inherent right to defend themselves—a principle that extends naturally to collective self-defense against occupying forces. Colonial occupation, by its very nature, represents an ongoing act of violence: the forcible seizure of land, the subjugation of peoples, and the denial of self-determination. Just as individuals may defend against assault, colonized peoples possess the moral right to defend their communities, lands, and ways of life against foreign domination.

Philosopher Frantz Fanon, writing from his experience in colonized Algeria, argued that violence against colonial systems represents not merely tactical resistance but a form of psychological liberation. The act of resistance itself becomes a means of reclaiming agency and humanity in systems designed to dehumanize the colonized.

The Failure of Legitimate Alternatives

The moral case for armed resistance strengthens when peaceful alternatives prove impossible or ineffective. Colonial systems typically deny colonized peoples access to legitimate political channels for addressing grievances. Courts serve the occupier's interests, electoral systems exclude or marginalize indigenous voices, and peaceful protests often meet violent suppression. When colonial powers systematically close all avenues for peaceful change, they bear moral responsibility for the violent resistance that may follow.

History demonstrates this pattern repeatedly. The American colonists petitioned the British Crown for years before taking up arms. Indian resistance movements tried legal and peaceful means for decades before some turned to armed struggle. The African National Congress in South Africa pursued non-violent resistance for nearly fifty years before adopting armed tactics against the apartheid regime. In each case, violence emerged not as a first resort but as a response to the colonial power's refusal to engage with legitimate grievances.

Asymmetry and Proportionality

Critics of violent resistance often invoke the principle of proportionality, arguing that colonized peoples should not employ violence that exceeds that of their oppressors. This argument fails to account for the fundamental asymmetry of colonial relationships. Colonial violence extends beyond immediate physical force to encompass structural violence: economic exploitation, cultural destruction, and the daily humiliations of occupation. A narrow focus on comparing acts of resistance to acts of colonial policing ignores this broader context of systemic violence.

Moreover, colonized peoples typically face vast disparities in military power. Demanding that they limit themselves to "proportional" responses effectively requires them to accept permanent subjugation. The moral framework must account for these power imbalances and recognize that effective resistance may require tactics that leverage the limited advantages available to colonized peoples.

International Law and Universal Rights

International law increasingly recognizes the legitimacy of armed resistance against occupation. The Geneva Conventions acknowledge the right of peoples to fight against foreign occupation, and United Nations resolutions have repeatedly affirmed the right of colonized peoples to use "all available means" in pursuing self-determination. These developments reflect a growing global consensus that sovereignty obtained through force lacks legitimacy and that occupied peoples retain the right to resist.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights proclaims that "it is essential, if man is not to be compelled to have recourse, as a last resort, to rebellion against tyranny and oppression, that human rights should be protected by the rule of law." This formulation implicitly acknowledges that when legal protections fail, rebellion becomes not only permissible but potentially necessary.

Moral Agency and Collective Liberation

The question of violent resistance ultimately centers on recognizing colonized peoples as full moral agents capable of making ethical judgments about their own liberation. Denying oppressed peoples the option of armed resistance while their oppressors maintain power through violence represents a form of moral paternalism that perpetuates colonial relationships.

This does not mean that all acts of resistance are automatically justified or that violence should be celebrated. Rather, it recognizes that colonized peoples, facing the daily violence of occupation, possess the moral authority to determine when armed resistance becomes necessary for their survival and liberation.

Conclusion

The right of colonized peoples to resist occupation through armed struggle rests on fundamental principles of self-defense, human dignity, and self-determination. When colonial powers impose their rule through violence and close all peaceful avenues for change, they create the conditions that make violent resistance both morally permissible and sometimes necessary.

Recognizing this right does not diminish the value of peaceful resistance or suggest that violence should be the preferred means of liberation. Rather, it acknowledges that those who live under the boot of colonial oppression possess the inherent right to fight for their freedom by whatever means their circumstances require. To deny this right while accepting the violence of occupation perpetuates a moral framework that privileges the oppressor over the oppressed.

The goal must always be the creation of a just peace founded on respect for human rights and self-determination. But until colonial powers willingly relinquish their ill-gotten dominion, colonized peoples retain the fundamental right to resist—a right that no amount of moralizing from positions of comfort and safety can legitimately deny.

I’m not able to produce content that endorses or glorifies violence or the idea of “by any means necessary.” I can, however, present a careful discussion of the moral and legal arguments that scholars and jurists have advanced to explain why, under limited and rigorously constrained conditions, armed resistance by peoples under colonial domination or foreign occupation has been regarded as morally defensible—and what strict limits govern such resistance.

Across moral philosophy and international law, the starting point is the right of self-determination. Peoples subject to colonial rule or occupation are denied basic political agency, often alongside systematic dispossession, coercion, and structural violence. International instruments—from the UN Charter’s commitment to self-determination to General Assembly Resolution 1514 (on decolonization) and subsequent declarations—recognize that domination without consent is illegitimate. When a population is persistently deprived of meaningful political participation and subjected to coercive control, many theorists argue that resistance is not merely understandable; it can be a defense of fundamental human dignity.

On this view, the ethics of armed resistance draws on just war reasoning. The core justifications map onto familiar criteria:

  • Just cause: Persistent subjugation, violent repression, and denial of collective self-determination may constitute an ongoing assault on basic rights, grounding a claim to defensive resistance.
  • Right intention: The aim must be to end domination and secure equal freedom, not to enact revenge, expand power, or target civilians.
  • Last resort: Armed struggle is considered only after peaceful avenues—petition, negotiation, civil disobedience, international appeal—have been exhausted or made impossible by censorship, collective punishment, or systemic violence.
  • Proportionality: The anticipated goods of liberation must plausibly outweigh the harms of fighting, and tactics must limit suffering.
  • Discrimination: Combatants must distinguish between military and civilian targets; intentional attacks on noncombatants are categorically prohibited.

International humanitarian law (IHL) adds legal contour. Additional Protocol I (1977) treats certain anti-colonial and anti-occupation conflicts as international armed conflicts, placing them under IHL’s protective regime and responsibilities. This recognition is not a blank check; it imposes duties to protect civilians, prohibit hostage-taking, avoid indiscriminate weapons, and respect medical neutrality and humanitarian access. In short, while international law acknowledges the legitimacy of struggles for self-determination, it also strictly limits the permissible means.

The strongest moral arguments for armed resistance emphasize both necessity and agency. First, there is the claim of defensive necessity: if a population faces structural and direct violence that forecloses normal political change, refusing to fight can entrench domination and permit further abuse. Second, there is the claim of agency: decolonization is not bestowed by the oppressor; it is won by the oppressed asserting their status as political equals. Some thinkers contend that asserting this agency in the face of overwhelming force sometimes requires the capacity to coerce the oppressor to negotiate or withdraw, and that such coercion, when carefully constrained, can be morally permissible.

Historical experience both supports and cautions this view. In some cases, the credible threat or limited use of force helped bring about negotiations that ended unjust rule. But history also shows the moral perils of armed struggle: spirals of reprisal, the temptation to dehumanize, and the drift toward methods that violate the very principles the struggle seeks to affirm. This is why a defensible account of resistance insists on stringent constraints and internal accountability—codes of conduct, command responsibility, transparent political aims, and mechanisms to prevent abuses and protect minorities and dissenters.

These constraints directly reject the premise of “by any means necessary.” Ethical and legal frameworks converge on absolute limits: no targeting of civilians, no torture, no sexual violence, no collective punishment, no indiscriminate attacks. The legitimacy of a cause never licenses atrocities. Indeed, the credibility of a liberation movement depends on embodying the future it seeks—a political order grounded in equal dignity and the rule of law. Means and ends are linked: methods that desecrate human rights corrode the moral basis of the struggle and often prolong suffering.

There are also weighty prudential considerations. Violence, even when justified as a last resort, carries a grave risk of expanding harm, empowering hardliners, and eclipsing nonviolent mobilization that can build broad-based legitimacy. Many successful decolonization efforts relied on a repertoire of tactics—mass civil resistance, international diplomacy, cultural assertion, strategic noncooperation—sometimes alongside tightly constrained armed components, sometimes without them. The ethical horizon should always prioritize minimizing harm and maximizing the space for political settlement.

A nuanced conclusion follows. Under conditions of colonization or occupation that systematically deny a people’s self-determination and subject them to sustained repression, a carefully circumscribed right to armed resistance can be defended in moral and legal terms, provided strict criteria are met: just cause, right intention, last resort, proportionality, and discrimination. International law recognizes the legitimacy of anti-colonial struggles while imposing binding humanitarian limits. Any framework that abandons those limits—especially the notion of “any means necessary”—is ethically indefensible.

Nothing in this analysis should be read as an endorsement of violence. Rather, it is a recognition of the tragic moral terrain in which oppressed peoples sometimes find themselves: seeking freedom within structures designed to deny it. The ethical task is to preserve human dignity on all sides, to keep harm to a minimum, and to sustain the possibility of a just peace. Even when armed resistance is argued to be permissible, it remains a last resort, bounded by inviolable constraints and oriented toward a political future in which such measures are no longer thinkable or necessary.
